content.p: Harshad Mehta was a Mumbai stockbroker who became known as the "Big Bull" in the early 1990s. In 1992 he was at the centre of a securities scam that shook the Bombay Stock Exchange and left several Indian banks holding receipts that had lost their value. He died in 2001, while his cases were still being heard, and courts convicted other people in connection with the scam in the years that followed.

Business Standard traced Mehta's path from a chawl in the central suburbs of Mumbai to the trading floor. He came from Raipur, which became the capital of the new state of Chhattisgarh. By the late 1980s he had become, in the paper's words, the bellwether of the Indian stock market. In the run-up to the 1992 crash he concentrated on a few counters, including ACC and Apollo Tyres, and drove their prices to levels that the paper described as unbelievable before they fell sharply.

According to Business Standard, the Sensex rose by about 4,200 points from under 800 in twelve months during the boom. Mehta's group used the money it could borrow in the banking system to buy obscure shares as well, among them Karnataka Ball Bearings and Mazda Leasing. The 2008 article wrote that in 1990 and 1991 nobody could say where his supply of money came from.

The scheme depended on a form of short-term lending between banks. A 2008 article, drawing on the book The Great Indian Scam, explained that a ready forward deal was in essence a secured loan from one bank to another, typically for about fifteen days. The borrowing bank sold government securities to the lender and bought them back at the end of the period at a slightly higher price.

In practice, the securities often did not move. The seller gave the buyer a bank receipt, which confirmed that the securities were held in trust for the buyer. Mehta needed receipts that were not backed by securities. According to the same 2008 article, two small banks, the Bank of Karad and the Metropolitan Co-operative Bank, issued such receipts for a fee. Other banks then paid money against them, believing they were lending against government paper.

Business Standard described the same mechanism in its 2012 retrospective. Money was drawn out of the inter-bank market and sent into the stock market, where chosen shares were pushed up. The money was returned when the shares were sold at a profit. The arrangement worked only as long as prices kept rising. Once they stopped, the banks were left holding receipts that had lost much of their value.

The 2008 article dates the public exposure to 23 April 1992, when the journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote a column in The Times of India describing how Mehta was drawing money from the banking system to finance his buying. Business Standard's 2012 retrospective argued that the questioning of Mehta in April 1992 left lasting marks: the bond market was slowed in its growth, and the country moved toward wider reform of market regulation, which gave the Securities and Exchange Board of India the powers it needed.

The Central Bureau of Investigation arrested Mehta on 9 November 1992, together with his brothers Ashwin and Sudhir. Business Standard reported the CBI's allegation that the three had misappropriated Rs 250 crore through 2.7 million shares of 90 blue-chip companies that had been described as lost or stolen. Harshad and Ashwin had claimed the shares were lost or stolen, and sought to have the custodian restore them to their account. The CBI, according to the same report, obtained confessions which it said showed that the family had transferred the shares to relatives, associates and employees and later reintroduced them into the market as benami holdings.

Mehta was held in judicial custody in Thane. Business Standard reported that on 21 December 2001 a special court had rejected his bail plea and his brothers' plea, and remanded them to custody until 4 January 2002. He was 47. Police sources told the paper that he complained of chest pain around 11 pm on a Sunday night and was taken to Thane civil hospital, where he died at 12.40 am. Hospital officials said he collapsed while a doctor was examining him. He was survived by his wife, two sons and two brothers.

The time of death in that account comes from police sources. A 2008 article said that, when he died, only one of the many cases filed against him had ended in a conviction. Business Standard's 2017 report said the case against him had been abated because he died during the trial.

On 25 November 2016 the Bombay High Court, in a judgment by Justice Shalini Phansalkar Joshi, convicted six of ten accused in the scam case, LiveLaw reported. Mehta's brother Sudhir was sentenced to six months' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 50,000. His cousin Deepak received four years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 3 lakh. Three officials of the National Housing Bank were also convicted. Three of the accused, along with a cousin, Hiten, who had been 19 at the time, were acquitted. The court suspended its verdict for eight weeks so that the convicted men could appeal to the Supreme Court.

The case began with a complaint that the National Housing Bank's deputy general manager, Manoj Kumar Rakshit, lodged with the CBI on 10 July 1992. It alleged a loss of Rs 1,214.30 crore to the bank, caused by cheques issued for ready forward transactions without the securities or bank receipts that should have backed them. The 2016 judgment dealt with only part of that sum, nine of the transactions. LiveLaw quoted the court's observation that the scam had been so damaging that at least two banks, the Bank of Karad and the Metropolitan Co-operative Bank, went into liquidation, and that millions of investors lost their savings and took nearly three years for the market to recover.

In April 2017 a special CBI court in Mumbai, under Special Judge H S Mahajan, convicted four former bank officials in another strand of the case. Business Standard named them as M S Srinivasan, a former funds manager of the State Bank of Saurashtra; Vinayak Deosthali, a former assistant manager of UCO Bank; R Sitaraman, an official of the State Bank of India's security wing; and P A Karkhanis, a former senior manager at UCO Bank. The four were charged with corruption, criminal breach of trust and falsifying books of account, and the prosecution said that they had acted to benefit the stockbroker. Each was fined Rs 5,000 and sentenced to three years, but was granted bail to appeal. A fifth accused, P S Gokhale, was acquitted. The case against Mehta and M V Shidhaye was abated because both had died during the trial. According to the prosecution, Rs 198 crore had been moved from the State Bank of Saurashtra to Mehta through call-money transactions recorded as though the counterparty were UCO Bank.

On 14 January 2003 the Supreme Court, by a 2-1 bench, upheld a conviction in a separate case over diverted funds of Maruti Udyog deposited with Canara Bank, which The Times of India reported had been routed to Mehta's account. The paper also reported that Mehta had died awaiting a hearing on his appeal, and that the court had reduced the sentence to the time already served. One of the three judges, M B Shah, would have acquitted all the accused, the paper said.

The loss figures in the public record do not agree. The 2008 article, quoting The Great Indian Scam, put the amount the banking system lost at Rs 4,000 crore. The Times of India reported that the Janakiraman committee, appointed by the Reserve Bank of India to examine the scam, quantified it at Rs 4,300 crore in its first report, a figure that involved units of the Unit Trust of India. The same paper's 2003 Supreme Court report described the scam as an Rs 8,000-crore securities scam. The National Housing Bank complaint alleged Rs 1,214.30 crore in its own case. Each of these figures is quoted from the paper that reported it, and none has been reconciled with the others in the pages reviewed.

Business Standard's 2012 retrospective argued that the scam had a lasting effect on Indian finance. The paper said that the fear that intermediaries would behave like Mehta, and that their manipulation would become standard market practice, kept controls on the bond market in place for years. It said the absence of a liquid bond market was still a problem in 2012, and that the scandal had helped push the Securities and Exchange Board of India toward the powers of a modern regulator. The same piece noted that Mehta's flamboyant public image, as the Big Bull, had made his fall a question about the culture of the early 1990s as much as about one man.

The cases that followed show how long the scam lasted in the courts. Mehta's own case was abated when he died, while other accused were convicted in 2016 and 2017. The loss figures quoted in the reports reviewed here remain far apart, from Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 8,000 crore.
